I am 65 years old and have been farming these lands in Quzhou for 40 years. My family has six mouths, but my son and daughter-in-law work off-farm in the city, and the grandchildren are in school, so it is mainly my wife and me in the fields. I have to be smart with labor — my back is not what it used to be. I keep 14 mu total. The wheat-maize double crop is my bread and butter; I will put 11 mu into that system because it is reliable and I can manage the tight harvest-planting window in June. I will plant 2 mu of garlic in October — it brings good cash at the market, but it is heavy work at planting time, so I need my wife's help. I save my own garlic cloves from last year, so I do not need to buy seed. I keep 1 mu of cotton because the price has been decent, but I will not expand it — too much spraying and picking for an old man.

For wheat, I will use improved seed and do rotary tillage before planting in early October. The extension agent said 15 kg nitrogen per mu, but fertilizer prices went up again last spring, so I will put about 13 kg per mu and add some compound fertilizer for phosphorus and potassium. I will irrigate three times — green-up, jointing, and grain-filling — because the well water is there but pumping costs electricity. For summer maize, there is no time to plough after wheat harvest; everyone in the village does no-tillage planting now. I will use hybrid seed and put fertilizer down at sowing. I will irrigate twice if June and July stay dry. Garlic needs more water and more potash to swell the bulbs, so four irrigations and a bit more K for that plot. Cotton gets less fertilizer overall because the plot is small, but I will spray seven times for bollworms and weeds — cotton is a pesticide-hungry crop and I cannot afford to let the worms ruin it. I am not chasing record yields; I want stable harvests that do not break my back or my wallet.
